lead: A USART is a universal synchronous/asynchronous receiver transmitter. The 8251 turns a parallel byte into a timed serial frame and back. The CPU writes a byte; the chip adds a start bit, optional parity and stop bits, then shifts the bits out on one pin at a fixed baud rate. In the other direction it finds the start bit, samples the data bits, checks parity and hands a clean byte to the CPU. It is used for RS-232 links, modem lines and simple two-wire board-to-board connections.
prereq: You need Unit 4, serial communication and RS-232 levels: baud rate, start and stop bits, and line levels.

blocks.text: A USART is a universal synchronous/asynchronous receiver transmitter. The 8251 is the classic programmable USART. The CPU side is parallel: D0-D7, C/D, CS, RD and WR. The line side is serial: TXD sends bits out, RXD receives bits in. A transmit buffer and transmit shift register form the outgoing path. A receive shift register and receive buffer form the incoming path. The CPU writes a byte; the shift register adds the frame and clocks it out one bit at a time. Received bits shift in and wait in the receive buffer.

C/D = 0 selects data; C/D = 1 selects control or status. TXRDY means the transmit buffer is empty. TXE means the shift register is empty too. RXRDY means a received byte is waiting. SYNDET is for synchronous mode. TXC and RXC are clock inputs; in async mode both TXC and RXC are 1, 16 or 64 times the baud rate.
The modem block has RTS (output), CTS (input), DTR (output) and DSR (input). CTS must be active before the 8251 transmits. In a board-to-board link these pins are often tied active.

An asynchronous frame sits on an idle-high line. A low start bit wakes the receiver. Data follows, least significant bit first. An optional parity bit follows. One or more high stop bits end the frame. The receiver samples each bit near its middle. A framing error means the stop bit was not high.
The mode word sets the frame. It is written to the control port after reset.

blocks.where: f<sub>TXC</sub> is the transmit clock in Hz; baud rate is bits per second; factor is 1, 16 or 64. For 9600 baud and 16×, f<sub>TXC</sub> = 153600 Hz.

blocks.text: The command word enables the directions and controls handshake. D0 = transmit enable. D2 = receive enable. D3 = send break. D4 = error reset. D5 = RTS. D6 = internal reset. D1 = DTR. D7 = hunt mode in synchronous mode. For transmit, receive and error reset, D0 = D2 = D4 = 1, giving 0001 0101 = 15H = 21 decimal.

The status word reports D0 TXRDY, D1 RXRDY, D2 TXE, D3 parity error, D4 overrun error, D5 framing error, D6 SYNDET and D7 DSR. Overrun means a new byte arrived before the old one was read. Framing means the stop bit was low. Parity means the parity bit did not match. The error reset command bit clears these three flags.

items: Power up: write 00H to the control port three times.
Write 40H to the control port. D6 = 1 is internal reset.
Write the mode word to the control port.
Write the command word to the control port.

blocks.text: The 8251 pins are TTL: 0 V and 5 V. RS-232 uses negative logic and about ±3 V to ±15 V. A MAX232 driver/receiver converts both ways and generates the negative voltage with a charge pump. Connect TXD and RXD through the driver/receiver.

examples.question: An 8251 is mapped at port 80H for data and 81H for control. Configure it for asynchronous operation at 9600 baud, 8 data bits, no parity, 1 stop bit, with a 16× clock. Give the reset sequence, the mode word, a command word that enables transmit and receive and resets errors, and the required TXC frequency.
steps: Reset: write 00H to 81H three times, then write 40H to 81H. 40H = 0100 0000; D6 = 1 is internal reset.
Mode fields: D7D6 = 01 for async 1 stop; D5 = 0 for no parity; D4 = 0 even/odd (don't care when parity is off); D3D2 = 11 for 8 data bits; D1D0 = 10 for 16×. Mode word = 0100 1110 = 4EH = 78 decimal.
Command fields: D0 = 1 transmit enable; D2 = 1 receive enable; D4 = 1 error reset; other bits 0. Command word = 0001 0101 = 15H = 21 decimal.
examples.answer: Write 00H three times, then 40H for reset; write mode word 4EH (78), then command word 15H (21); TXC must be 153600 Hz (153.6 kHz).
examples.check:
baud = 9600
factor = 16
mode = (0b01 << 6) | (0b11 << 2) | (0b10 << 0)
cmd = (1 << 0) | (1 << 2) | (1 << 4)
print(baud * factor)
print(mode)
print(cmd)

traps: The mode word is accepted only after the reset sequence. If you write a command first, the chip can sit in an unknown state and the first characters disappear with no error flag.
C/D selects data against control/status. Writing a mode word to the data port is ignored.
In the standard 8251A, D7D6 = 01 is async 1 stop, 10 is 1.5 stop and 11 is 2 stop. 8EH is a 1.5-stop mode word, not 8N1.
TXRDY means the transmit buffer is empty. TXE means the shift register is also empty. Poll TXRDY before writing the next byte.
Parity, overrun and framing flags are cleared by the error reset command bit D4 = 1, not by reading the status word.

quiz.q: Why does an asynchronous frame need a start bit?
quiz.a: The line is idle high. A low start bit tells the receiver a frame is beginning and lets it align its sampling clock.

quiz.q: Find the 8251 mode word for asynchronous 7 data bits, even parity, 2 stop bits and a 64× clock.
quiz.a: D7D6 = 11 for 2 stop; D5 = 1 parity enable; D4 = 0 even; D3D2 = 10 for 7 bits; D1D0 = 11 for 64×. Mode word = 1110 1011 = EBH = 235 decimal.

quiz.q: A status read gives TXRDY = 1, TXE = 0, RXRDY = 1 and OE = 1. What happened and what should the CPU do?
quiz.a: TXRDY = 1 means the transmit buffer is empty and ready for a new byte. TXE = 0 means the shift register is still busy sending the last byte. RXRDY = 1 with OE = 1 means overrun: a new byte arrived before the old one was read and a received byte was lost. The CPU should read the received byte, issue the error reset command (D4 = 1) to clear the overrun flag, and service RX faster.

quiz.q: Which 8251 modem pins are outputs and which are inputs?
quiz.a: Outputs: RTS and DTR. Inputs: CTS and DSR.

quiz.q: Find the TXC frequency for 19200 baud with a 64× factor.
Why is a MAX232 needed between the 8251 and an RS-232 connector?
quiz.a: The 8251 uses 0/5 V TTL levels. RS-232 uses negative logic and about ±3 V to ±15 V. The MAX232 converts levels and generates the negative supply.

beyond: Not for the exam. Modern boards use UARTs such as the 16550 or a microcontroller UART, often behind USB-CDC. RS-485 extends the same UART frame over twisted pair for factory floors. Linux exposes these ports through termios settings. Search '16550 UART', 'MAX485', 'USB CDC ACM' and 'termios baud rate'.
